title: Using Water Droplet Reactor Strategy to Directly Observe Disassembly Process of Pt Micelle in Liquid Phase Transmission Electron Microscopy
content: The decoration of nanoparticles with surfactants has long been a crucial strategy for tailoring surface properties, enabling precise control over dispersion, stability, and interfacial interactions [1] Surfactants broadly encompass molecules that modify the surface of nanoparticles through covalent and non-covalent interactions, playing a fundamental role in preventing aggregation and enhancing colloidal stability [2]. This control is essential for diverse applications, including catalysis, energy conversion, sensing, biomedical imaging, and nanomaterial synthesis. In catalytic systems, surfactants can act as ligands, selectively stabilizing crystal facets and altering electronic properties to influence reactivity and selectivity [3]. In sensing applications, surfactant coatings can be used to precisely functionalize probe materials, enhancing their targeting specificity [4]. For example, a gold surface functionalized with glutathione (GSH) molecules can effectively detect lead ions in wastewater [5]. Additionally, individual nanoparticles can spontaneously assemble into metamaterials with superlattices and precisely engineered architectures, enabling the creation of novel materials with unprecedented properties [6-7]. Despite the widespread and significant applications of surfactants in nanomaterial decoration and functionalization, challenges persist in understanding and optimizing surfactant-mediated nanoparticle interactions, particularly regarding the direct observation of micelle formation and disassembly dynamics, as well as unlocking the underlying mechanistic kinetics.
